stem: Why does a computer need **secondary storage**?

options.content: To store programs and data permanently, because RAM is volatile
options.rationale: Correct: secondary storage is non-volatile.

options.content: To hold the instruction that the CPU is executing right now
options.rationale: That is held in a register (the CIR).

options.content: To run the bootstrap program when the computer is switched on
options.rationale: The bootstrap runs from ROM.

options.content: To speed up the CPU by storing frequently used instructions
options.rationale: That describes cache.

explanation: RAM loses its contents when the power is off, so files and programs are kept on non-volatile secondary storage.

stem: Which type of storage has **no moving parts**?

options.content: Solid-state
options.rationale: Correct: flash memory stores data electronically.

options.content: Magnetic hard disk drive
options.rationale: An HDD has spinning platters and a moving arm.

options.content: Blu-ray disc in a drive
options.rationale: Optical discs spin in a drive and are read by a moving laser.

options.content: DVD in a drive
options.rationale: DVDs spin and are read by a moving laser.

explanation: SSDs, SD cards and USB flash drives use flash memory: no moving parts.

stem: In a hard disk drive, how is data written to the platter?

options.content: A laser in the read/write head burns tiny pits into the surface of the platter
options.rationale: Pits and lands are used on optical discs.

options.content: Electrons are trapped on floating gates in transistors
options.rationale: That is how flash memory works.

options.content: Ink is sprayed onto the platter in a pattern
options.rationale: No ink is used in storage devices.

options.content: An electromagnet in the read/write head magnetises tiny areas of the surface
options.rationale: Correct: the direction of magnetisation represents 1 or 0.

explanation: Magnetic storage: read/write heads use electromagnets to magnetise areas of the platter.

stem: How is data read from an optical disc?

options.content: A read/write head detects the direction of magnetised areas on the disc
options.rationale: That describes a hard disk.

options.content: The charge on each floating gate is measured by the drive
options.rationale: That describes flash memory.

options.content: A laser is shone on the disc and the different reflections from pits and lands are detected
options.rationale: Correct: changes in reflected light are converted to binary.

options.content: A camera photographs the disc and software decodes the image
options.rationale: Optical drives use a laser and a light sensor, not a camera.

explanation: Optical storage: a laser reads the spiral track of pits and lands.

stem: In flash memory, where are electrons trapped to store data?

options.content: On the control gate
options.rationale: The control gate's voltage moves electrons onto the floating gate.

options.content: On the magnetic platter
options.rationale: Platters are part of a hard disk.

options.content: On the floating gate
options.rationale: Correct: the insulating layer keeps them there without power.

options.content: In the pits of the disc
options.rationale: Pits belong to optical discs.

explanation: Each flash cell has a control gate and a floating gate; trapped charge on the floating gate represents a bit.

stem: Why can a Blu-ray disc store much more data than a DVD of the same size?

options.content: It spins much faster than a DVD, so the drive can fit many more tracks onto the disc
options.rationale: Spinning speed affects reading speed, not capacity.

options.content: It stores data magnetically instead of by using pits and lands
options.rationale: Blu-ray is optical, like a DVD.

options.content: It uses flash memory chips hidden inside the disc
options.rationale: A Blu-ray disc has no flash memory.

options.content: Its blue-violet laser has a shorter wavelength, so smaller pits can be packed closer together
options.rationale: Correct: smaller pits mean more data per track.

explanation: Shorter wavelength → smaller focused spot → smaller, denser pits → higher capacity.
hints: What is different about the laser?

stem: A company in Harare must back up 20 TB of records every week as cheaply as possible. Speed is not important. Which medium is most suitable?

options.content: SD cards
options.rationale: Their capacity is small and the cost per gigabyte is high for 20 TB.

options.content: CDs
options.rationale: Hundreds of thousands of CDs would be needed.

options.content: Magnetic hard disk drives
options.rationale: Correct: very large capacity at a low cost per gigabyte.

options.content: USB flash drives
options.rationale: Higher cost per gigabyte and smaller capacity than hard disks.

explanation: HDDs give large capacity at a low cost per gigabyte, which suits bulk backups.
hints: Which storage is cheapest for very large amounts of data?

stem: Why are laptops increasingly built with SSDs rather than HDDs?

options.content: SSDs are always cheaper per gigabyte than HDDs, so they lower the laptop's price
options.rationale: SSDs usually cost more per gigabyte.

options.content: SSDs have no moving parts, so they are faster, lighter, use less power and survive knocks
options.rationale: Correct: all of these matter for a portable computer.

options.content: SSDs store data magnetically, so they are not affected by magnetic fields at all
options.rationale: SSDs store data electronically, not magnetically.

options.content: SSDs can be rewritten an unlimited number of times without ever wearing out
options.rationale: Flash cells have a limited number of write cycles.

explanation: No moving parts: fast access, low weight and power, durable when carried. The trade-off is a higher cost per gigabyte.
hints: Think about what happens to moving parts when a laptop is dropped or carried.

stem: The CPU can directly access data stored on a hard disk drive without loading it into RAM first.
explanation: False. Secondary storage is not directly accessed by the CPU; data is loaded into RAM first.

stem: Each surface of a hard disk platter is divided into tracks, and each track into sectors.
explanation: True. Data is located by its track and sector.

stem: Match each storage medium to the type of storage.
explanation: HDD: magnetic. CD, DVD, Blu-ray: optical. SSD, SD card, USB drive: solid-state.

hints: Use the parts of a hard disk drive.

stem: A USB flash drive holds 64 GiB. Each music file is 8 MiB. How many music files can be stored? (Ignore space used by the file system.)
hints: Convert GiB to MiB by multiplying by 1024.

stem: A Blu-ray disc holds 25 GB. A teacher wants to copy recorded lessons of 3 GB each onto it. How many whole lessons fit on the disc?
hints: Only whole files fit: round down.

stem: On an optical disc, the tiny hollows formed by the laser are called pits. What are the flat areas between them called?
explanation: Optical discs store data as pits and lands on a spiral track.

stem: Describe how solid-state (flash) memory stores data. [4]

points.description: Uses NAND or NOR technology / made of transistors arranged in cells
Each cell has a control gate and a floating gate
A voltage on the control gate moves electrons onto the floating gate, where they are trapped (by an insulating layer)
Whether charge is trapped or not represents 0 or 1; it stays without power, so it is non-volatile

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Flash memory uses NAND or NOR cells built from transistors. Each cell has a control gate and a floating gate. Applying a voltage to the control gate pushes electrons onto the floating gate, where they are trapped by insulation. Trapped or not trapped charge represents a 0 or 1, and it remains when the power is removed.

explanation: Transistors, control and floating gates, trapped electrons, non-volatile.

stem: Sipho is a freelance video editor in Bulawayo. He films on location with a small camera, edits on a laptop and keeps an archive of all his finished projects.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Match each use to the most suitable storage.

left.content: Main drive in the editing laptop

parts.explanation: SD card: tiny and robust; SSD: fast; HDD: cheap per GB.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe how data is read from the hard disk drive used for the archive.

points.description: The platters spin and the arm moves the read/write head over the correct track
The data is located by track and sector
The head detects the direction of magnetisation of each area, which represents 1 or 0

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The platters spin while the arm moves the read/write head over the right track. When the sector passes underneath, the head detects the direction in which each tiny area is magnetised; one direction represents 1 and the other 0.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain **two** reasons why an SSD is better than an HDD for editing on the laptop.

points.description: Faster access to data (no moving parts), so large video files open and save quickly
More durable when the laptop is carried / lighter / uses less power, so the battery lasts longer

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: With no moving parts, the SSD reads and writes the large video files much faster, and it is not damaged if the laptop is knocked while it is being carried to locations.

explanation: SD card, SSD and HDD each suit a different need; HDD reading uses spinning platters, heads and magnetised areas.
hints: Choose by capacity, speed, cost, durability and portability.
Use the parts of each technology when describing how it works.

stem: A school office in Mutare stores letters and reports on a 2 GB flash drive and keeps older records on DVDs.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Each document is 0.5 MB. Using 1 GB = 1024 MB, calculate how many documents fit on the flash drive.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which type of storage is a DVD?

options.content: Magnetic
options.rationale: That is a hard disk.

options.content: Optical
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Solid-state
options.rationale: That is flash memory.

options.content: Primary
options.rationale: A DVD is secondary storage.

parts.explanation: DVDs are optical: read by a laser.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Give **two** reasons why the flash drive is more suitable than a DVD for documents that are changed every day.

points.description: Data can be rewritten easily many times / DVDs are often write-once or slow to rewrite
Faster to access / more durable (no scratches) / more portable / larger capacity

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The flash drive can be rewritten quickly every day, whereas a DVD is slow to write and often can only be written once; the flash drive is also not damaged by scratches.

explanation: 4096 documents; DVD is optical; flash drives are rewritable, fast and durable.
hints: Compare the media using durability and capacity.
